title: the golden deer
hook: the deer leads Rama deeper and deeper into the forest, and with its last breath it speaks in his voice
carry: a voice in the wrong mouth

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana saw through the golden deer, Sita longed for it, and Rama went after it, telling Lakshmana not to leave her.

Rama takes his bow, buckles on his sword, and goes. The deer lets him get close, then bounds away. It vanishes into the trees, then appears again in a clearing, glowing, waiting. It runs, stops, looks back. Valmiki says it seemed to be playing with him: sometimes near, sometimes far, sometimes gone altogether. And every time it reappears, it's a little farther from the hut, from Sita, and from Lakshmana.
screen: `CLOSE, THEN GONE.` → `IT LOOKS BACK, WAITING.` → `FURTHER FROM THE HUT.`

segments.voice: At last Rama is tired, angry, and very far from home. He stops trying to catch it. He fits an arrow, blazing like a snake, the text says, and shoots. The arrow strikes the deer in the heart, and as it falls, the disguise falls away. On the ground lies Maricha, huge and bleeding, his real shape back. With his last breath he does the one thing left of Ravana's plan. He cries out in a perfect copy of Rama's voice: Ha Sita! Ha Lakshmana! Then he dies. Standing over the body, Valmiki says, Rama is afraid. He remembers Lakshmana's words: it's Maricha, it's a trick. Now he sees the rest of it. If Sita hears that cry, what will she think? What will she make Lakshmana do? He turns and runs back toward Panchavati as fast as he can. Pause on Maricha. He warned his king, confessed his fear, and went only under threat of death. He dies by Rama's arrow, as he said he would. Many devotional tellings say that, dying at Rama's hand with Rama's name on his lips, Maricha was released. Valmiki just tells what happened: a voice in the forest, saying a name, in the wrong mouth.
screen: `AN ARROW TO THE HEART.` · `THE DISGUISE FALLS AWAY.` · `HA SITA! HA LAKSHMANA!` · `RAMA, AFRAID, RUNS BACK.` · then, large: `A VOICE IN THE WRONG MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a voice you trust, someone's way of saying your name, and hear it clearly. Then let the voices go quiet and listen only to your own breath, the plainest sound you have. Each time a voice comes back in your head, return to the breath.
Maricha. The deer's disguise falls away when Rama's arrow strikes, and he dies crying out in Rama's voice: Ha Sita! Ha Lakshmana!
Your line: a voice in the wrong mouth. Back at the hut, Sita hears it. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: The golden deer's cry in Rama's voice is one of the best-known moments of the Ramayana, staged in Ramlila and retold in many languages as the turning point before Sita's abduction.

fork.setup: you're Rama. the deer has led you far away. it won't let you catch it. what do you do?
options: give up and walk home slowly.
fork.reveal: he shoots. the disguise falls away, and Maricha dies crying out in Rama's voice.

trapdoor: what you thought: the golden deer is just a pretty animal Rama hunts.
what it means: it's Maricha, who dies calling out in Rama's voice to finish Ravana's plan.
what a scholar hears: Aranya 44 ends with Rama's fear; later devotional tellings add that Maricha was released by dying at Rama's hand.

chat.says: What made the golden deer trick actually work on Rama's family?

The deer led Rama so deep into the forest that he got lost and couldn't come back.

chat.meaning: Struck by Rama's arrow, Maricha used his last breath to cry Ha Sita! Ha Lakshmana! in Rama's voice, the last piece of Ravana's plan.

Maricha.meaning: the rakshasa disguised as the golden deer

Panchavati.meaning: the place of five banyans, where the hut stands

Ravana.meaning: the king of Lanka, who planned the trick

Lakshmana.meaning: Rama's younger brother, who shares his exile

recall: the mountain of their first forest home

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 44 (the chase; Maricha's death; the cry)

notes: 'Ha Sita! Ha Lakshmana!' renders the Sanskrit cry (hā sīte, hā lakṣmaṇa); not a quotation of any translation.
The arrow 'blazing like a snake' paraphrased; confirm.
Some editions have Rama kill another deer and carry its meat back after Maricha's death; omitted here.
Maricha's release at death is attributed to devotional tellings, not Valmiki; confirm.
